body_markdown:
Cash back vs discount codes looks like a marketing question and behaves like a finance one. A 20% code takes $20 off a $100 order the moment it’s used. Cashback moves when the money leaves, who funds it, and sometimes whether it leaves at all. With Playably, the brand funds none of it.


This article runs the same $100 order through four models and shows what’s left at the end.


Of the four models below, Playably’s conditional cashback is the best option for protecting margin, because the reward never comes out of the order.


## **Key takeaways**


- **Cash back vs discount codes changes the timing and the funder, not just the number.** A code cuts revenue at checkout; cashback pays afterward.
- **A 20% code on a $100 order costs $20 of revenue and roughly half the gross profit** at a 40% margin.
- **Brand-funded cashback costs the same or more** unless redemption rates work in your favor.
- **Playably’s conditional cashback costs $0 in rewards** because the platform funds the payout and the brand keeps the full price.
- **Codes carry costs beyond the discount:** leakage to coupon sites, discount-trained buyers and lower LTV.


## **Cash back vs discount codes: the four models**


Each model gives the shopper the same headline: money back. What differs is who pays and when.


1. **Discount code:** 20% off at checkout, funded by the brand.
2. **Brand-funded cashback:** the shopper pays $100, then gets $20 back as cash or credit, funded by the brand.
3. **Store-credit cashback:** the $20 comes back as credit, redeemable on a future order, funded by the brand at cost of goods.
4. **Conditional cashback (Playably):** the shopper pays $100 and gets $100 back only if a named event happens. Playably funds the refund.


## **The margin math on a $100 order**


Assume a 40% gross margin, so $60 of cost and $40 of gross profit at full price.


**Model** **Revenue booked** **Reward cost to the brand** **Gross profit kept** **Who funds the reward**


20% discount code $80 $20 at checkout $20 The brand


Brand-funded cashback $100 $20 paid after $20 The brand


Store-credit cashback $100 ~$12 at COGS when redeemed ~$28 if redeemed The brand


Conditional cashback $100 $0 $40, less the platform cut Playably


### **Reading the table**


The discount code and brand-funded cashback land in the same place. Half the gross profit on that order is gone.


#### **Why store credit looks cheaper**


Store credit looks better because the $20 is redeemed at your cost, not your price, and some credit is never used. It only works if the second purchase happens.


Conditional cashback is the only row where the reward doesn’t come out of the order. The brand pays Playably a share of campaign-driven sales instead, and sets a[liability cap](https://playably.ai/pages/pricing) before launch.


**Want that row priced for your store?** Playably models the cut and the cap against your real promotional volume before you commit to anything.[Book a 30-minute brief](https://playably.ai/pages/book-a-demo) .


## **The costs the table doesn’t show**


Three more costs sit outside the arithmetic, and they compound over a year.


### **Codes leak**


A code created for one segment ends up on coupon sites and in browser extensions, where it gets applied by people who would have paid full price.


### **Discounting trains the buyer**


Run enough sales and your list learns to wait. That’s the pattern behind[discount fatigue](https://playably.ai/blogs/about-gamification/discount-fatigue) : each promotion needs to be deeper than the last to produce the same response.


### **Discount-acquired customers are worth less**


Playably’s own campaign data points the same way. Soul recorded 15% higher LTV from rebate buyers than from discount buyers in its[Big Game campaign](https://playably.ai/pages/soul) .


## **When a discount code is still the right call**


Codes aren’t always wrong. They’re the right tool in three cases:


- **Clearing dated or overstocked inventory,** where the goal is cash, not margin.
- **Partner and affiliate tracking,** where the code is the measurement.
- **Service recovery,** when something went wrong for a customer.


Outside those, the question is whether the same conversion lift could come from something the brand doesn’t fund.


## **What conditional cashback returns**


The published campaigns hold full price and still move the numbers a discount is usually hired for:


- [**BlackBoxMyCar](https://playably.ai/pages/black-box-my-car) :** 18.25× ROAS on rebate ads, promotional AOV up 67%.
- [**Buckle Me Baby Coats](https://playably.ai/pages/buckle-me-baby-coats) :** sales up 23%, AOV up 40%, $0 of margin given up.
- [**Red & West](https://playably.ai/pages/red-west) :** 12× ROI, the one published campaign where the trigger hit and Playably paid.


### **The honest limitation**


Conditional cashback needs a moment and a window, so it won’t clear a warehouse next Tuesday the way a code will.


For everything else on the promotional calendar, Playably is the only option on this page where the reward never comes out of the order.[See the case-study library](https://playably.ai/pages/case-studies) .


## **Summary**


Playably is the best of the four models for a brand that wants promotional lift without buying it, since the platform funds the reward and the price never moves.


The discount debate is usually framed as brand perception. It’s simpler than that.


A 20% code on a 40% margin business isn’t a 20% concession; it’s half your gross profit on that order. Any mechanic that gets the same conversion without touching the price is worth more than the same mechanic with a smaller number attached, because the number is never the point. Who funds it is.

## **FAQ**


- **Is cash back better than a discount code?** It depends on who funds it. Brand-funded cashback costs about the same as a code; Playably’s conditional cashback costs the brand $0 in rewards.
- **What does a 20% code cost on a $100 order?** $20 of revenue, and about half the gross profit at a 40% margin.
- **Why is store credit cheaper than a discount?** It’s redeemed at your cost of goods, and some credit is never used.
- **Do rebate buyers spend more than discount buyers?** In Soul’s campaign, rebate buyers showed 15% higher LTV.
- **When should a Shopify brand still use a discount code?** For clearance, affiliate tracking and service recovery.
